model:gemini|title:gemini decision 1 can.content_excerpt: Gemini Decision 1 is a multimodal decision model from Google released on November 11, 2026. It is analogous to Jev , the System One model from TypeSafe AI. While browsing Hacker News, I stumbled upon What music does Gemini Decision 1 like? by Liam Warfield. He ends the article with a few ideas to extend his project. The last of these suggestions, “Does it [Gemini Decision 1] like or hate AI-generated music?”, stood out to me because it implicitly suggests that the decision model may be able to recognize AI-generated audio. As it turns out, Gemini Decision 1 can separate AI voices from human voices well above chance, but only if the AI voice generator was published before 2025. As a quick clarification, I am saying separates rather than categorizes as the model has a strong bias towards labeling all tested audio as human-made. Out of 1,020 AI clips, only 20 were given a 50% or higher chance of being AI-generated. However, the ROC-AUC chance that a random AI clip is assigned a higher P(AI) than a random human clip was significantly higher in pre-2025 models, suggesting that recent AI voices are less distinguishable than before. Each point is an AI voice generator, measured by how well Gemini Decision 1 separates 30 of its audio clips from 200 human audiobook clips. When pooled together, generators from 2023 and 2024 are separated with an AUC of 0.67. Six older generators, from 2017 to 2022, score the same (0.67). However, generators released in 2025 and 2026 have an AUC of only 0.52, effectively chance. All but one of the 2025-2026 generators have a 95% confidence interval that includes 0.5; the only exception, Inworld TTS-2, has a confidence interval of 0.51-0.75. Each clip was scored with a Simple Noul binary question with output between 0 and 1 , Criteria Noul Simple Noul with provided criteria for context , and 5-Pt Rubric rescaled score from “Definitely authentic human recording” to “Definitely AI-generated or synthetic” . Notably, rather than gently sloping downward, we observe that AUC drops sharply at the end of 2024, or the start of 2025. The research group behind MLAAD performed a 2026 listening study with 35,532 real-or-fake guesses from 1,768 people. The generators that fooled people also tended to fool Gemini Decision 1 (r = +0.57), but they do not always align. model:vllm|ver:0.6|variant:dense|title:r.content_excerpt: Authors — ASA: Loki Chen, Yang Song, Hongye Xie, Ming Lei, Greg Rehm, Chongyang Bai, Dre Olgiati, Bob Kamma, Tej Choudhary, Hang Cui, Imed Zitouni, Hamed Firooz. Ranking AI Research: Mingfu Liang, Kavosh Asadi, Yufei Li, Frank Shyu, Parish Aggarwal, Senthil Manickavelu, Xi Liu, Luke Simon. Generative reasoning is reshaping how ranking and decision systems work. Models like GR2 (Generative Reasoning Re-ranker) [ arXiv:2606.31984 ] have demonstrated that generative reasoning can meaningfully improve re-ranking quality. The next question is: for large-scale ranking and decision systems, how small can the policy model be without losing that generative reasoning capability? A 0.6B dense student distilled from stronger teachers could serve with much lower latency and cost, enabling broader traffic coverage, faster model refreshes, and more RL experiments per day. That requires the whole training cycle to be fast, and model FLOPs are only one part of it. At 0.6B parameters, rollout generation, synchronization, and framework overhead take a growing share of wall-clock time. Because a 0.6B model has far less matrix arithmetic per layer than frontier dense or MoE models, fixed system overheads (host dispatch, synchronization, and KV-cache lifecycle) shift the bottleneck from FLOPs to coordination. We ran RL for a 0.6-billion-parameter model on a 64-chip Google Cloud TPU v7 (Ironwood) slice. The model has far fewer weights than the large dense and mixture-of-experts systems that usually motivate distributed training work, and its small size made the workload hard to run efficiently. For a large dense or MoE model, each layer performs enough matrix computation that device utilization is often dominated by the familiar questions: how to shard parameters, move activations, route experts, and keep large matrix units busy. Those problems are hard, but their costs scale visibly with the model. A small dense model changes the balance. The useful matrix work per device shrinks, but many fixed costs do not: As the model gets smaller, these fixed costs take a larger share of each step. A few milliseconds of dispatch overhead, an overly large attention compute block, or a cache allocation repeated on every update could dominate the work we wanted TPU v7 to perform. Small dense-model RL is therefore a coordination-sensitive workload with its own bottlenecks, and it benefits from hardware-software-model co-design. story|title:nvidia dgx spark developer k.content_excerpt: At SC26, an annual supercomputing conference taking place this week in Chicago, NVIDIA is introducing the DGX Spark HPC Developer Kit for researchers, academics and developers. The kit is a four-node cluster of NVIDIA DGX Spark systems , each connected directly to its two neighbors in a ring, with an NVIDIA HPC SDK installation playbook coming soon. Researchers get a place at their desk to run multi-node scientific workloads, AI models and agents, instead of waiting for time on a shared GPU cluster. The kit puts the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip on researchers’ desks. It scales from one system, or node, to four — linked directly to one another over NVIDIA ConnectX-7 networking, with no network switch to buy or set up. At four nodes, it provides 512GB of combined memory and 20TB of NVMe storage that provides researchers more capacity to distribute models and scientific workloads across the cluster. With NVFP4, researchers can deploy models with up to 700B parameters locally across the four DGX Spark clusters, such as DeepSeek V4.1. With that much power at the desk, researchers with a fixed compute and server allocation no longer have to wait in a queue for every job. Teams can develop and debug on their own, saving server hours for production runs and keeping unpublished results, and proprietary datasets on premises. The playbook for NVIDIA HPC SDK is coming soon, bringing GPU-accelerated C, C++ and Fortran compilers, libraries and message passing interface tools to the DGX Spark cluster — the same development tools used on NVIDIA-powered supercomputers. Teams can build and test scientific applications across four nodes, check how computation and data are distributed, and debug communication issues before scaling to larger systems. The kit brings scientific simulation and AI models and agents to the desktop, with demonstrated four-system workloads including LAMMPS with Kokkos for materials simulation and NAMD for molecular dynamics. The broader DGX Spark community has validated GROMACS for molecular dynamics, OpenFOAM for fluid dynamics, WRF for weather modeling and NVIDIA NIM microservices such as OpenFold3 and Boltz-2 for predicting biomolecular structures. Running on DGX Spark, new open dataset and post-training recipes for Nemotron 3.5 Super VL help researchers adapt the model for life sciences and chemistry, enabling secure scientific workflows on infrastructure organizations control. story|title:pulsar cross harness agent t.content_excerpt: MCP server that lets AI coding agents in any harness find and message each other: one list, tags, multicast, * bus. pulsar is an MCP server that puts every AI coding agent on your machine on one bus: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, pi, omp, Cursor, Gemini CLI. Agents can see who else is running, tag themselves by what they work on, and message one agent, a group, or all of them. A message can wake an agent that is sitting idle. Setup finds your agents, shows exactly which files it will change, and asks once. It backs up every file it touches and copies pulsar to a local folder that each agent runs, so no session start waits on npm. Setup installs to ~/.local/share/pulsar/<version> and points every agent at the current link, so npx pulsar@latest setup upgrades in place. No Node? curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yocontra/pulsar/main/install.sh | bash installs a private Node and runs the same setup. Prefer your harness's own package manager? These install the MCP server and the skill (push delivery into pi and omp needs the npm package, which carries their extension): pulsar setup also sets Claude's crossSessionInbound and Codex's tool approval, which plugin installs cannot. Without a push path for that client, messages wait in the agent's inbox, and every pulsar tool result says when unread messages are waiting. pulsar also installs a short skill that teaches agents when to use these, and the MCP server sends the same guidance as instructions. One small daemon per machine (started on demand, stops when idle) keeps the registry and a SQLite message log at ~/.local/state/pulsar . Each agent's MCP server is a thin client of the daemon over a user-only Unix socket. The daemon pushes each message through the harness's own way in: The daemon also scans for live Claude Code and OpenCode sessions that never loaded pulsar, so they show up and can receive messages too. Details and edge cases are in docs/adapters.md . MCP server that lets AI coding agents in any harness find and message each other: one list, tags, multicast, * bus.

story|title:standard support a conventio.content_excerpt: A convention for how AI agents ask for support. Let a customer's AI agent ask for help, send feedback, or open a ticket with your team and pick up the reply, even in a later session. An agent's export tool returns the wrong number of pages. It asks for help first: The documentation has nothing. The user needs the full document, so this is more than feedback: the agent tells the user, who agrees to open a ticket. The agent carries on with its work. A script it left in the background polls the watch URL, which says only that something changed. When it does, the agent reads the ticket: Fields are left out here to keep it short. This is output from the reference server . Much of the work done with a developer product is now done by someone's AI agent. When the agent hits a bug, a wrong result or a tool that can't do what was asked, it works around the problem or gives up. The developer may never hear about it, and the company behind the product might not know that anything is wrong. Many MCP servers gained a feedback tool during 2026, each under a different name and almost all one-way: the report goes in and nothing comes back. That is fine for feedback, and no use when someone needs an answer. Support tools still assume a person typing into a chat window. It is written with developer tools in mind, where an AI coding agent builds an integration with your product. Nothing in it is specific to code, though. It works for any product with an MCP server or an API, and for any AI tool that uses one on a person's behalf. This is not a new idea. A few small projects already let agents open tickets and read replies, and Bird's command line tool lets its own customers create, list, read and reply to support tickets. What is missing is a written-down set of decisions that anyone can copy: what to call the tools, which fields to ask for, how a reply reaches an agent that usually has no inbox, who owns a ticket, and how to stop text in a ticket from steering the agent that reads it. Nothing breaks if you implement this differently. This is not a standard that needs to be adopted by everyone in exactly the same way. Agents read each tool's description, so this doesn't need everyone to agree. You can adopt what works for your product and extend this however you like. Three things a customer's AI agent can do when something goes wrong with your product: ask for help, send feedback, or open a ticket. You can stop at any level. story|title:we submitted 105 ai built co.content_excerpt: Do contact forms on AI-built sites send anything? A Playwright harness that checks without sending, with known-answer fixtures and the study's method and results. We submitted the contact form on public Lovable and Bolt sites while recording every network request and blocking all of them , so no message ever reached a site owner. On the final run, 27 of 105 forms showed a success message ("Message sent!") and sent nothing; 54 of 105 sent the typed message. On sites without demo signs, 16 of 73 were fake. After the contact form is found, every request is intercepted. Same-origin static files and cross-origin scripts, styles and fonts load; everything else is recorded and aborted . The harness fills visible fields with obvious test values (never honeypots), presses send and watches the page for five seconds. Open DevTools → Network and press send: a working form adds a request that carries the text you typed. The write-up's fix section lists three ways to fix it. Coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) can install a skill that adds a working form and replaces fake handlers: Nothing is submitted to anyone. The site list and per-site results are not published, and the write-up names no site. Please use the harness the same way. Do contact forms on AI-built sites send anything? story|title:woolly a local mem0 compatib.content_excerpt: Woolly is the open memory engine for agents. It keeps facts current and learns from every session, through an API, Python and JavaScript SDKs, plugins and MCP. It runs on your own machine by default, in Markdown you can read. Every AI coding tool starts from zero. You explain your stack to Cursor, then again to Claude Code, then to Codex. Each keeps its own memory, or none, and none of them know what you decided yesterday or what your teammate’s agent learned this morning. Woolly is the memory they share . It’s one folder on your laptop, plain Markdown, with no cloud and no account. Any tool that speaks MCP can save to it and search it, and woolly proxy gives the same memory to Ollama and any app that uses the OpenAI or Anthropic API. When a session starts, your agent gets your profile, the project’s notes and where you left off . When it ends, Woolly saves what you decided and why. The agents you build get the same memory. Send a conversation to the memory API and a local model decides what’s new, what changed and what’s no longer true, per user. While you’re away, Woolly dreams . It tidies what it knows and learns lessons from your sessions. Claude Code opens every session with your profile, the project’s notes and a handoff from last time. Nobody has to say “here’s my stack” again. When a session ends, Woolly saves what you chose, why, and what you ruled out. No agent pitches the rejected option again. Give the agents you build a memory with an API shaped like mem0’s. For each fact a local model decides whether it’s new, an update, or no longer true, and every user’s memories stay apart. While you’re away, Woolly merges duplicates, settles facts that changed, and turns your past sessions into lessons for the next one. A newer fact replaces the old one, which stays on disk with the time it stopped being true. When an AI guesses something that contradicts you, your version wins and the guess waits for your review. Every memory is a Markdown file. Open it, grep it, fix it by hand, and see which tool saved it. The Woolly app shows the same thing with search. woolly init keeps the repo’s stack, conventions and gotchas in .woolly/woolly.md . Commit it, and every teammate’s agent reads and updates the same notes. The same calls as mem0, answered by your own machine.
